clue.text: Rule from South-East wanted by its nationalists? Just the reverse

definitions.text: Rule from South-East wanted by its nationalists? Just the reverse

parts.words: Rule from South-East wanted by its nationalists? Just the reverse
parts.note: a land in the west of Britain whose nationalists do not want to be governed from London in the South-East; they want home rule

explanation.surface: Nationalists seem to be clamouring for government from the South-East, until the clue flips it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue pretends nationalists want rule from the South-East (London); the reverse is true: they want rule from their own country. The South-East is the region of England around London, seat of the UK government.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh nationalists campaign for self-government rather than control by Westminster in London's South-East.

clue.text: Young man advised to go thus from Harrow to Oxford?

definitions.text: Young man advised to go thus from Harrow to Oxford?

parts.words: Young man advised to go thus from Harrow to Oxford?
parts.note: echoes the saying 'Go west, young man', and Oxford lies west of Harrow in north-west London

explanation.surface: A public schoolboy from Harrow is told which way to head for university.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is a school in north-west London; Oxford is to its west, and the old advice was 'Go west, young man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling from Harrow to Oxford heads towards the setting sun, the direction in the famous advice to young men.

clue.text: Happy old Scotswoman

explanation.surface: Describes a cheerful elderly woman from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots, lucky (or luckie) is a familiar term for an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortunate is one sense, and in Scots dialect it is a familiar name for an elderly woman.

clue.text: Changes to another's style of furniture

indicators.note: changes made to the following word mean its letters are rearranged

parts.note: here the letters of the word are used in full, including the S

explanation.surface: Someone switches to a different person's taste in furnishings.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of ANOTHERS are rearranged. Thomas Sheraton was an 18th-century English furniture designer.
explanation.definitionFit: A neoclassical English style of chairs and cabinets is named after the designer Thomas Sheraton.

clue.text: Deep depression — full of drink, perhaps

explanation.surface: Someone sinks into a deep depression after a heavy night drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A hollow in hills is called a punch bowl, and the bowl itself holds the party drink of punch.

clue.text: Prepare cases for a collection of suits

explanation.surface: Getting the luggage ready for a set of business clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Filling suitcases is packing, and a deck of playing cards with its four suits is a pack.

clue.text: Fresh enthusiasm, and source of 15

parts.note: fresh means new
zeal is eager enthusiasm
taken as written

explanation.surface: New eagerness is the origin of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is the rugby team at 15-down, which comes from this country.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous rugby side named at 15 is the national team of this Pacific country.

clue.text: Wealthy man supports bit of fireside chat

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece that supports another sits beneath it, so it comes second

parts.note: a hob is a shelf beside a fireplace
a nob is a rich or upper-class person

explanation.surface: A rich man props up some cosy talk by the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to socialise and talk familiarly, a synonym for informal conversation.

clue.text: Not on green, perhaps, yet below par

explanation.surface: A golfer off the green is playing below standard.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: not on a colour such as green; the second means slightly unwell. 'yet' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally away from a hue such as green, and idiomatically feeling slightly ill.

clue.text: Install a serious piece of scientific equipment

indicators.note: piece of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An instruction to install a substantial bit of lab kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A device emitting a focused beam of light is standard laboratory apparatus.

clue.text: Unassailable counterpart of Papal bull?

parts.note: a bull is a male bovine and also a decree from the Pope; the female animal held holy and beyond criticism is its partner

explanation.surface: Asks what matches a Pope's decree in being beyond challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea or institution treated as beyond criticism is a revered animal of the female kind, matching the bovine pun on a Papal bull.

clue.text: More than one enthusiast shines

explanation.surface: A group of fans spends the afternoon polishing something.
explanation.definitionFit: Fans of a hobby are buffs, and to polish to a shine is to buff.

clue.text: What highwaymen do is, with respect, unprofessional

parts.note: a way is a respect, as in 'in some ways' meaning in some respects
lay means not belonging to a profession, as a layman

explanation.surface: Someone politely suggests that robbers on the road are amateurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is only a link joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Highway robbers ambush travellers on the road, lying in wait to attack them.

clue.text: No time to start an operation?

definitions.text: No time to start an operation?

parts.words: No time to start an operation?
parts.note: read 'No time' as nothing plus a time period, and the phrase also names the moment a military operation begins

explanation.surface: Someone protests there is no time to begin surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Nought plus a unit of time gives the phrase for the scheduled moment an attack or operation begins.
explanation.definitionFit: The planned starting moment of a military attack is labelled with a nought, as in countdown parlance.

clue.text: Vehicle at school? That's one way to travel

parts.note: a cab is a taxi, a vehicle
in can mean at, as in 'in school'
a class is a group taught together at school

explanation.surface: Someone takes a taxi to school as their way of getting there.
explanation.definitionFit: A grade of passenger accommodation on a liner is a manner of making a journey.

clue.text: Like deeds of a traitor beheaded — that's fair

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter is cut off the word that the traitor phrase gives

parts.note: acts of a traitor are treasonable

explanation.surface: A traitor's punishment by beheading is declared just.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' takes the T off TREASONABLE; 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean just or moderate, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Fifteen involved in perfect display of potter's skill

definitions.text: involved in perfect display of potter's skill

explanation.surface: Fifteen people somehow involved in a master craftsman's pottery show.
explanation.walkthrough: The rugby team of New Zealand is a fifteen; in snooker a maximum 147 break pots a black after each of the fifteen reds. The potter is a snooker player, not a ceramicist.
explanation.definitionFit: New Zealand's rugby union fifteen bears the name, and a maximum snooker break pots every dark ball worth seven.

clue.text: Chancy way to raise a little money

explanation.surface: A gamble seems an easy way to make some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: tossing a coin raises a small piece of money into the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Flipping a coin decides things by chance, and that flip throws a coin upward.

clue.text: Marshals? They have a job handling crooks

definitions.text: They have a job handling crooks

explanation.surface: Lawmen are said to have work managing criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: The crooks are shepherds' hooked staffs, not criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: To marshal a group is to guide it along, and flock-keepers carry hooked staffs as part of their work.

clue.text: Pursuing first part of 15, despite everything

parts.note: pursuing someone is going after them

indicators.note: first part of takes the opening word of the two-word answer at clue 15

parts.note: the answer at 15-down, the New Zealand rugby team

explanation.surface: Chasing something to the end regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word of the 15-down answer gives ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'in the end' or 'nevertheless' expresses the same idea as regardless of what happened.

clue.text: Wise old Greek doesn't reach conclusion on his own

indicators.note: failing to reach the end means the final letter of the Greek's name is dropped

parts.note: Solon was the Athenian lawgiver, proverbially wise

explanation.surface: An ancient philosopher fails to finish his argument without help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't reach conclusion' drops the last letter N from SOLON.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting alone is acting solo, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Opera, if not funny, might be grand

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd, so the letters of the preceding words are reworked

explanation.surface: An opera that fails to be comic might still be magnificent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' rearranges the letters of OPERA IF NOT; 'might be' signals the definition is an example: a grand is a kind of piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand is a large concert keyboard instrument, one type of the full-named piano.

clue.text: Running problem a streaker doesn't have

explanation.surface: Describes a runner's ailment that a naked dasher avoids.
explanation.walkthrough: A streaker runs naked, so they have not a stitch on.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp side pain hits joggers, and a single sewn loop of clothing is what a naked runner lacks.

clue.text: Into which Lord Lundy was shoved "towards the age of twenty-six" (Belloc)

definitions.text: Into which Lord Lundy was shoved "towards the age of twenty-six" (Belloc)

parts.words: Into which Lord Lundy was shoved "towards the age of twenty-six" (Belloc)
parts.note: Hilaire Belloc's cautionary verse says the weepy Lord Lundy was pushed into a career in government at about twenty-six

explanation.surface: A literary quiz question about Belloc's comic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Belloc's Cautionary Tales tell of Lord Lundy, who cried too easily and was therefore sent into public life in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's line has Lundy shoved into the world of government and Parliament.

clue.text: Just like Bunter to take fruit pie that's missing

parts.note: a plum is a fruit

indicators.note: missing means the letters for 'that's' are taken away from the word pie

parts.note: taken as written
ie is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A greedy schoolboy grabs a fruit pie that has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the fat schoolboy of British comic stories. 'missing' removes IE (that is) from PIE, leaving P; 'to take' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunter is famously overweight, so rotund or chubby fits him.

clue.text: Sort of chaser that will do for hunt

indicators.note: sort of suggests a version of the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A kind of chaser is all that is needed for a hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges CHASER; 'that will do for' links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To hunt for something is to look for it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: It detects a bandit coming up or going down

indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads identically upwards or downwards, as palindromes do

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A device spots an enemy aircraft whether it climbs or dives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bandit' is airmen's slang for an enemy aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio detection equipment locates hostile planes, which pilots call bandits.

clue.text: This dog's a point above the rest, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word for a summit is said aloud

parts.note: a peak is the highest point, standing above the rest

explanation.surface: This dog is reckoned a cut above the others.
explanation.walkthrough: PEKE is short for Pekingese, a small dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pekingese toy breed is commonly shortened this way.

clue.text: Not abridged like some new books

explanation.surface: A complete text, like many freshly printed volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: Old books were sold with folded pages not yet slit apart, so a new copy could have untrimmed leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A full text has nothing removed, and a book whose page edges are still folded is likewise not trimmed.

clue.text: Nine so-called Popes, including the English one

definitions.text: Nine so-called Popes, including the English one

parts.words: Nine so-called Popes, including the English one
parts.note: a papal name borne by eight Popes and an antipope, so nine claimants in all, and also a common English first name

explanation.surface: A history question about a run of pontiffs with the same name.
explanation.walkthrough: Popes took this name eight times plus one antipope, hence 'so-called'; 'the English one' is the ordinary English form of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight pontiffs and one antipope reigned under the papal name rendered in English as this.

clue.text: Get to the pass somehow with expedition

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive in some unstated order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller must reach the mountain pass quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges TO THE PASS; 'Get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with expedition means with speed, as does going with great haste.

clue.text: Ground swells?

explanation.surface: Asks whether the land is rising.
explanation.walkthrough: LORD'S is the famous London cricket ground; swells are toffs, and peers are such toffs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord's is London's headquarters of cricket, and peers of the realm are upper-class grandees.
